tweets.text:
I saw a design team's OKRs recently, and it made me so sad....

"Run 5 research studies"

"Deliver designs for 8 initiatives"

You could tell someone had passed down the edict from on-high that everyone needed them, and they *needed* #s.

not an original thought, but "limiting WIP" confuses people

it is actually
-increase focus
-limit multi-tasking
-stop starting, start finishing
-collaborate more
-try to keep less things in memory
-reduce planning inventories
-increase flow
-learn faster
-pivot earlier

hunch

prioritizing backlogs/roadmaps is WAY LESS important that prioritizing strategic pillars, high-level inputs/value drivers, what not to do, NoKRs, etc

product tip

what a Facebook product manager does or doesn't do is 95% irrelevant for you (unless you work at Facebook)

understanding what the current source of drag is in YOUR COMPANY, and figuring out where to find inspiration for safe experiments is much more important.

Most teams jump from high level strategy/goals straight to feature ideas (w/ "success metrics")

The most successful teams
1. Have a strategy
2. Translate that into models
3. Add minimally viable measurement
4. Identify leverage points
5. Explore options
6. Run experiments

product managers...imagine that your title actually reflected what you did all day...

what is your real-world title?

Something I’ve learned the hard way

You can facilitate an amazing activity.

But if there’s no follow up ppl will blame the activity vs their inability to invest time in the follow up.

Facilitating the follow up is some crazy high % of any activity.

What specific behaviors do you observe in people who are “more strategic” ?

More specific than “better strategies”.

Day to day objective behaviors.

product manager tip

also every designer (of interfaces, systems) is skeptical about "iterating" because they've been subject to a "its good enough, ship it" (and never come back to it)

if you want ppl to embrace "shipping and learning", you NEED to make room for improvement

product takes a village

design, design research, development (across different areas), data expertise, marketing,  product management, (and many more)

...the idea that product = product management is very limiting.
